tool.name: webpack
tool.tagline: Configurable module bundler that builds a dependency graph into optimized bundles
tool.description: webpack is the module bundler that powered a decade of frontend development: starting from entry points it builds a dependency graph of JavaScript, CSS and assets, transforms them with loaders and plugins, and emits optimized bundles. It still runs a huge number of production applications and enterprise build pipelines, and its concepts (loaders, code splitting, module federation) underpin newer tools such as Rspack.

concepts.name: What webpack does
concepts.summary: webpack starts from entry points, follows every import to build a dependency graph, and emits bundles the browser can load.
concepts.why: Many production apps still build with webpack, and its concepts explain how all bundlers work.
concepts.body:
Browsers load files over the network, while your code is split into hundreds of modules plus npm packages, CSS and images. A **bundler** turns that source tree into a few optimized files.

**webpack** works like this:

- Start from one or more **entry points** (e.g. `./src/index.js`).
- Parse each module and follow its `import`, `require()` and `import()` calls to build the **dependency graph**. CSS, images and fonts can be part of the graph too.
- Run each non-JavaScript (or non-plain-JavaScript) file through **loaders**, which turn it into modules webpack understands.
- Group modules into **chunks** and emit them as **bundles**, with a small **runtime** that loads modules and chunks in the browser.
- **Plugins** hook into every step for everything else: HTML generation, CSS extraction, minification, environment variables.

webpack 5 is extremely flexible, which is its strength and its cost: configuration can grow large, and builds are slower than Rust-based tools. New projects usually start with Vite or a framework's built-in tooling, while existing webpack apps often migrate to **Rspack**, a Rust reimplementation with a largely compatible API. The concepts in this course transfer directly to both.

The four core concepts to remember: **entry**, **output**, **loaders**, **plugins**, plus **mode** to choose development or production defaults.
concepts.code:
# Minimal setup: no config file needed for the defaults
mkdir wp-demo && cd wp-demo && npm init -y
npm install -D webpack webpack-cli
mkdir src
echo 'import { greet } from "./greet.js"; console.log(greet("Ann"));' > src/index.js
echo 'export const greet = (n) => `Hello, ${n}`;' > src/greet.js

npx webpack --mode production
# asset main.js 49 bytes [emitted] [minimized] (name: main)
# ./src/index.js + 1 modules ...
# webpack compiled successfully

node dist/main.js      # Hello, Ann
takeaways: Entry -> dependency graph -> chunks -> bundles
Loaders transform files; plugins hook into the whole build
Defaults: entry ./src/index.js, output dist/main.js
Rspack offers a webpack-compatible, faster alternative
pitfalls: Starting a new project with a hand-written webpack config when a framework or Vite would do.

quiz.q: What does webpack build before emitting any bundle?
options: A dependency graph starting from the entry points
quiz.explain: webpack follows imports from the entries to discover every module that belongs in the output.

concepts.name: Configuration: entry, output and mode
concepts.summary: Write webpack.config.js with entry, output and mode, use content hashes in filenames, and clean the output folder.
concepts.why: Every webpack project starts from this skeleton.
concepts.body:
`webpack.config.js` exports a configuration object (or a function returning one). The essentials:

- `entry`: a string, an array, or an object of named entries, e.g. `{ app: "./src/app.js", admin: "./src/admin.js" }` for two separate bundles.
- `output.path`: an **absolute** directory, usually `path.resolve(__dirname, "dist")`.
- `output.filename`: a template with placeholders: `[name]` (entry or chunk name), `[contenthash]` (hash of the file's content, for caching), `[id]`. For example `[name].[contenthash].js`.
- `output.clean: true`: empty the output directory before each build.
- `output.publicPath`: the URL prefix where assets will be served (`"/"` or `"auto"`).
- `mode`: `"development"` (readable output, fast rebuilds, helpful errors) or `"production"` (minification with Terser, tree shaking, scope hoisting, `process.env.NODE_ENV` set to `"production"`). Without a mode, webpack warns and assumes production.

Run with `npx webpack` (reads `webpack.config.js`), `npx webpack --config other.config.js`, or `npx webpack --mode development`. Put commands in npm scripts.

Exporting a **function** `(env, argv) => config` lets one file handle several modes: `argv.mode` holds the CLI mode and `--env foo=bar` arrives as `env.foo`.
takeaways: `entry` names bundles; `output.path` must be absolute
`[name]` and `[contenthash]` placeholders in filenames
`mode` switches on dev or production defaults
Export a function to vary config by mode and --env
pitfalls: Omitting `mode`, getting a warning and production defaults during development.

options: File names change only when content changes, enabling long-term caching
quiz.explain: Browsers can cache hashed files forever; new content gets a new name.

concepts.name: Loaders
concepts.summary: Transform files with module.rules: test, use and exclude, chain loaders right to left, and process CSS and modern JavaScript.
concepts.why: Loaders are how webpack handles anything beyond plain JavaScript.
concepts.body:
Out of the box webpack understands JavaScript and JSON. **Loaders** teach it other file types or transform code, configured in `module.rules`:

- `test`: a regex matched against the file path, e.g. `/\.css$/i`.
- `use`: one loader or an array of loaders (with `options` objects).
- `exclude` / `include`: limit which files a rule applies to, e.g. `exclude: /node_modules/` for Babel.

**Loader chains run right to left** (bottom to top). For CSS:

- `css-loader` resolves `@import` and `url()` and turns CSS into a JavaScript module.
- `style-loader` takes that result and injects it into the page via `<style>` tags.

So `use: ["style-loader", "css-loader"]` runs css-loader first. Add `"sass-loader"` at the end for Sass, or `"postcss-loader"` between them for autoprefixing.

Common loaders:

- `babel-loader` for modern syntax and JSX; alternatives `swc-loader` and `esbuild-loader` are much faster.
- `ts-loader` for TypeScript, or Babel/SWC to strip types and run `tsc --noEmit` separately.
- `css-loader` with `modules: true` (or files named `*.module.css` by default) for CSS modules.

Images and fonts no longer need loaders in webpack 5; they use asset modules (next lesson).
takeaways: `module.rules`: test + use (+ include/exclude)
Loader chains execute right to left
style-loader + css-loader for CSS; babel/swc/esbuild loaders for JS
Exclude node_modules from expensive transforms
pitfalls: Writing `["css-loader", "style-loader"]`, which feeds raw CSS to style-loader and fails.

quiz.explain: Loaders apply right to left, so Sass is compiled first, then css-loader, then style-loader.

concepts.name: Plugins: HTML, CSS extraction and defines
concepts.summary: Use HtmlWebpackPlugin to generate index.html, MiniCssExtractPlugin to emit CSS files, and DefinePlugin for compile-time constants.
concepts.why: Real apps need an HTML page, CSS files and environment values, all provided by plugins.
concepts.body:
**Plugins** are objects with an `apply(compiler)` method that hook into the build. You add instances to the `plugins` array.

The ones nearly every app uses:

- **HtmlWebpackPlugin** (`html-webpack-plugin`): generates `index.html` with `<script>` (and `<link>`) tags for the emitted bundles, including hashed names, optionally from your own template.
- **MiniCssExtractPlugin** (`mini-css-extract-plugin`): extracts CSS into separate `.css` files for production instead of injecting it with JavaScript. Use its `loader` in place of `style-loader`, typically only in production.
- **DefinePlugin** (built in, `webpack.DefinePlugin`): replaces expressions at compile time, e.g. `__API_URL__` or `process.env.API_URL`. Values are inserted as code, so wrap strings in `JSON.stringify`.
- **CopyWebpackPlugin**: copies static files that are not imported.
- **ProvidePlugin**, **BundleAnalyzerPlugin** (`webpack-bundle-analyzer`) and many more.

Built-in plugins live on the `webpack` object; third-party ones are npm packages. `mode` already adds several plugins for you (e.g. minification in production), so do not add them twice.

Like Vite's `VITE_` variables, anything you define ends up in the client bundle; never inject secrets.
takeaways: Plugins hook into the compiler for everything loaders can't do
HtmlWebpackPlugin writes index.html with the right script tags
MiniCssExtractPlugin emits CSS files in production
DefinePlugin inserts code: wrap strings in JSON.stringify
pitfalls: `new DefinePlugin({ API: 'https://x' })`, which inserts an unquoted URL as code and breaks the bundle.

quiz.q: Why wrap DefinePlugin string values in JSON.stringify?
options: Values are inserted as code, so strings need quotes
quiz.explain: DefinePlugin does textual replacement with code; JSON.stringify produces a valid string literal.

concepts.name: Asset modules: images, fonts and files
concepts.summary: Handle images, fonts and other files with webpack 5's built-in asset module types instead of file-loader and url-loader.
concepts.why: Every app ships images and fonts, and webpack 5 handles them without extra loaders.
concepts.body:
webpack 5 replaced `file-loader`, `url-loader` and `raw-loader` with built-in **asset modules**, selected with a rule's `type`:

- `asset/resource`: emits the file to the output directory and exports its URL (formerly file-loader).
- `asset/inline`: exports a data URI (formerly url-loader).
- `asset/source`: exports the file's contents as a string (formerly raw-loader).
- `asset`: chooses automatically: files under `parser.dataUrlCondition.maxSize` (8 KB by default) are inlined, larger ones emitted.

Output names come from `output.assetModuleFilename` (default `[hash][ext][query]`) or a rule's `generator.filename`, e.g. `images/[name].[contenthash][ext]`.

You can then `import logoUrl from "./logo.png"` in JavaScript, and `url(./bg.png)` in CSS is handled by css-loader through the same rules. `new URL("./file.png", import.meta.url)` also works and is the bundler-agnostic way.

Choosing between inline and resource is a trade-off: inlining saves a request but increases bundle size and bypasses separate caching; keep it for tiny icons. For SVGs used as React components, add `@svgr/webpack`. Remove old file-loader rules when migrating, or assets get processed twice.
takeaways: asset/resource = file + URL, asset/inline = data URI
asset/source = contents as string, asset = automatic by size
Name files via assetModuleFilename or generator.filename
Drop file-loader/url-loader when on webpack 5
pitfalls: Keeping legacy file-loader rules alongside asset modules, so files are emitted twice.

quiz.q: Which asset type inlines small files and emits larger ones?

concepts.name: webpack-dev-server and HMR
concepts.summary: Run webpack-dev-server for in-memory rebuilds, hot module replacement, API proxying and history API fallback for SPAs.
concepts.why: A fast feedback loop during development depends on the dev server setup.
concepts.body:
**webpack-dev-server** compiles your app in memory (nothing is written to `dist/`), serves it, and pushes updates to the browser over a WebSocket. Start it with `npx webpack serve`.

Configuration lives under `devServer`:

- `port`, `host`, `open`.
- `hot: true` (the default): **hot module replacement**. Changed modules are swapped in place when an HMR boundary accepts them; otherwise the page reloads (`liveReload`). CSS through style-loader updates instantly. For React, add `@pmmmwh/react-refresh-webpack-plugin` with `react-refresh` for state-preserving component updates.
- `static`: folders served as-is (like `public/`).
- `historyApiFallback: true`: serve `index.html` for unknown paths, required for client-side routers.
- `proxy`: an **array** of rules forwarding API calls to a backend: `[{ context: ["/api"], target: "http://localhost:8000" }]`.
- `client.overlay`: show build errors over the page.

In plain modules, the HMR API is `module.hot` (CommonJS style) or `import.meta.webpackHot` (ESM): `accept`, `dispose`, `invalidate`.

For server-rendered apps or custom servers, `webpack-dev-middleware` and `webpack-hot-middleware` integrate the same features into Express. Like any dev server, never expose it to the internet.
takeaways: `webpack serve` builds in memory and serves with HMR
historyApiFallback for client-side routing
proxy is an array of { context, target } rules
React needs react-refresh-webpack-plugin for Fast Refresh
pitfalls: Looking for dev-server output in dist/; it only exists in memory.

quiz.q: A React Router app shows 404 when reloading /settings in dev. Which option fixes it?
quiz.explain: Unknown paths must fall back to index.html so the client router can handle them.

concepts.name: Module resolution and aliases
concepts.summary: Control how imports are found with resolve.extensions, alias, modules, conditionNames and fallback for Node built-ins.
concepts.why: Import errors and duplicated packages usually come down to resolution settings.
concepts.body:
When webpack meets `import x from "something"`, its resolver (enhanced-resolve) decides which file that is. The `resolve` options shape that:

- `extensions`: suffixes tried for extension-less imports, e.g. `[".tsx", ".ts", ".js"]`. Keep the list short; every entry costs file-system lookups.
- `alias`: map a prefix to a path: `"@": path.resolve(__dirname, "src")`. A trailing `$` makes an exact match (`react$`). Aliases also force a single copy of a package, e.g. pointing `react` at one location in a monorepo. Mirror aliases in `tsconfig.json` `paths` for TypeScript.
- `modules`: directories searched for bare imports, default `["node_modules"]`.
- `conditionNames` and `mainFields`: which package.json `exports` conditions and legacy fields are honoured (`browser`, `module`, `import`, `require`...). The defaults depend on `target`.
- `fallback`: webpack 5 no longer polyfills Node built-ins like `crypto` or `buffer` for the browser. Either avoid them, provide polyfills (`fallback: { buffer: require.resolve("buffer/") }`), or disable with `false`.

`resolve.fullySpecified` relates to ESM packages, where relative imports must include the extension; errors like "fully specified" come from `.mjs` files or `"type": "module"` packages.

Debug with `npx webpack --stats=detailed` or by temporarily setting `infrastructureLogging: { level: "verbose" }`.
takeaways: `extensions`, `alias`, `modules` steer the resolver
webpack 5 does not polyfill Node built-ins: use `fallback`
Mirror aliases in tsconfig paths
Keep `extensions` short for speed
pitfalls: Expecting `require('crypto')` to work in browser code as it did with webpack 4's automatic polyfills.

quiz.q: After upgrading to webpack 5, a dependency fails with "Can't resolve 'buffer'". Why?
options: webpack 5 stopped auto-polyfilling Node core modules
quiz.explain: You must now add a `resolve.fallback` polyfill or replace the dependency.

concepts.name: Source maps and per-environment configs
concepts.summary: Pick a devtool for each mode, split config into common, dev and prod files with webpack-merge, and pass environment values.
concepts.why: Debuggable builds and maintainable configs both depend on these choices.
concepts.body:
**Source maps** map bundled code back to your sources in DevTools and error trackers. The `devtool` option picks the strategy, trading build speed against quality:

- `eval-cheap-module-source-map` (or `eval-source-map`): fast rebuilds with good mappings; typical for development.
- `source-map`: full, separate `.map` files; best quality, slowest. Use in production if you serve or upload maps.
- `hidden-source-map`: produces maps without the `//# sourceMappingURL` comment, so browsers do not download them but you can upload them to Sentry or similar.
- `false`: no maps (production default).

Words in the name mean: `eval` (each module wrapped in eval, fast rebuilds), `cheap` (line-only mappings), `module` (maps through loaders to original sources), `inline` (embedded as data URLs, never in production).

**Splitting config**: as configs grow, keep `webpack.common.js` and merge mode-specific files with `webpack-merge`, or export a function and branch on `argv.mode`. Pick one approach and stay consistent.

**Environment values**: read `process.env` in the config (Node), then expose only what the client needs through `DefinePlugin` or `EnvironmentPlugin`. `dotenv-webpack` loads `.env` files. Again: everything defined ends up in the bundle.
takeaways: Dev: eval-cheap-module-source-map; prod: source-map or hidden-source-map
`inline` maps never belong in production
webpack-merge composes common + mode-specific configs
EnvironmentPlugin/DefinePlugin expose only what the client needs
pitfalls: Shipping `eval` or `inline` source maps in production bundles.

quiz.q: Which devtool creates maps that browsers won't load but an error tracker can use?
quiz.explain: hidden-source-map omits the sourceMappingURL comment, so maps are not referenced publicly.

concepts.name: Code splitting and SplitChunksPlugin
concepts.summary: Split bundles with dynamic import(), magic comments and prefetching, and tune SplitChunksPlugin's cache groups for vendor code.
concepts.why: Shipping less JavaScript up front is the biggest lever for load performance.
concepts.body:
webpack creates separate **chunks** in three ways:

- **Entry points**: each entry is its own chunk (duplicating shared code unless you configure sharing).
- **Dynamic imports**: `import("./chart.js")` returns a promise and puts the module and its dependencies in a chunk loaded on demand. Route-level splitting with `React.lazy` uses this.
- **SplitChunksPlugin** (`optimization.splitChunks`): extracts shared modules and vendor code into common chunks.

**Magic comments** tune dynamic imports: `import(/* webpackChunkName: "chart" */ "./chart.js")` names the chunk, `webpackPrefetch: true` fetches it in idle time, `webpackPreload: true` loads it in parallel with the parent.

**SplitChunksPlugin** defaults apply to async chunks only. Set `chunks: "all"` to also split initial chunks, so vendor code shared by entries is loaded once. **Cache groups** define how modules are grouped:

- `defaultVendors` collects `node_modules` modules; `default` collects modules used by at least two chunks.
- Add your own, e.g. a `react` group for React packages with a higher `priority`.
- `minSize` (20 KB by default; smaller groups are not split out), `maxSize`, `minChunks`, `maxAsyncRequests` and `maxInitialRequests` limit how aggressive splitting is.

Inspect the result with `webpack-bundle-analyzer`. Too many tiny chunks cause request overhead; one giant vendor chunk invalidates the cache on every dependency update.
takeaways: Dynamic import() creates on-demand chunks
Magic comments: webpackChunkName, webpackPrefetch, webpackPreload
`splitChunks.chunks: 'all'` shares vendor code across entries
Cache groups with priorities control grouping
pitfalls: Prefetching everything, which wastes bandwidth on chunks users rarely need.

quiz.q: By default, which chunks does SplitChunksPlugin optimize?
quiz.explain: The default is `chunks: 'async'`; set 'all' to include initial chunks.

concepts.name: Long-term caching and persistent cache
concepts.summary: Keep hashes stable across builds with contenthash, a runtime chunk and deterministic ids, and speed up rebuilds with the filesystem cache.
concepts.why: Users should only re-download what changed, and developers shouldn't wait for unchanged work.
concepts.body:
Two different kinds of caching matter with webpack.

**Browser caching of outputs.** With `[contenthash]` in filenames, unchanged files keep their names and stay cached. To keep hashes truly stable:

- `optimization.runtimeChunk: "single"` moves webpack's small **runtime** (which contains the chunk-to-filename manifest) into its own file. Otherwise, adding a lazy chunk changes the manifest inside your main bundle and its hash.
- `optimization.moduleIds: "deterministic"` and `chunkIds: "deterministic"` (production defaults in webpack 5) keep ids stable when unrelated modules are added.
- Split rarely changing vendor code into its own chunk.
- Serve hashed files with `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`, and `index.html` without caching.

**Build caching.** `cache: { type: "filesystem" }` persists the module and chunk caches to `node_modules/.cache/webpack`, making second and later builds dramatically faster, including in CI if you cache that folder. Invalidate correctly with `cache.buildDependencies: { config: [__filename] }` so config changes reset the cache; `cache.version` lets you bump it manually. In development mode the default is an in-memory cache.

If builds behave strangely after dependency upgrades, delete the cache folder first.
takeaways: contenthash + runtimeChunk + deterministic ids = stable hashes
Vendor chunks change rarely and stay cached
`cache: { type: 'filesystem' }` speeds up rebuilds and CI
Declare buildDependencies so config changes invalidate the cache
pitfalls: Leaving the runtime in the main chunk, so every new lazy route changes the main bundle's hash.

options: The runtime's chunk manifest changes often and would change other bundles' hashes
quiz.explain: Isolating the manifest keeps the main and vendor hashes stable.

concepts.name: Tree shaking and sideEffects
concepts.summary: Get dead code eliminated with ES modules, usedExports, the sideEffects flag and scope hoisting, and know what breaks it.
concepts.why: Unused library code is often the largest part of a bundle.
concepts.body:
**Tree shaking** removes exports nobody imports. In webpack it is a cooperation of several steps, all enabled in production mode:

- `optimization.usedExports`: webpack marks which exports of each module are used.
- The minifier (Terser) then deletes the unused, now-unreferenced code.
- `optimization.sideEffects`: if a package declares `"sideEffects": false` in its `package.json`, webpack can skip **entire modules** whose exports are unused, even if they were imported through a re-exporting index file.
- `optimization.concatenateModules` (scope hoisting) merges modules into one scope, making the output smaller and faster.

What breaks it:

- **CommonJS** (`require`, `module.exports`): webpack 5 can analyze some patterns, but ESM is far more reliable. Make sure Babel does not convert ESM to CommonJS (`modules: false` in preset-env; the default with babel-loader is to keep ESM).
- **Side effects at module top level** (polyfills, global CSS imports, registering things). If you mark a package `"sideEffects": false`, list files that do have side effects: `"sideEffects": ["*.css", "./src/polyfills.js"]`, or your CSS disappears.
- Importing a whole namespace and using it dynamically (`lib[name]`).

Mark pure function calls with `/*#__PURE__*/` so minifiers can drop them when unused. Verify with the bundle analyzer, or by setting `usedExports` with `mode: "development"` and looking for `/* unused harmony export */` comments.
takeaways: Tree shaking needs ES modules
usedExports marks, the minifier removes
`sideEffects: false` lets webpack skip whole modules
List CSS and polyfills in sideEffects so they survive
pitfalls: Setting `"sideEffects": false` in an app that imports global CSS, silently dropping the styles.

quiz.q: Why can `"sideEffects": false` make global CSS imports disappear?
options: It only affects production source maps
webpack assumes unused imports with no side effects can be dropped, and a CSS import has no used exports
quiz.explain: CSS imports exist only for their side effect, so they must be listed in sideEffects.

concepts.name: Module Federation and micro-frontends
concepts.summary: Share code between independently deployed builds at runtime with Module Federation remotes, exposes and shared singletons.
concepts.why: Large organisations use it to compose apps from separately deployed micro-frontends.
concepts.body:
**Module Federation** (webpack 5's `ModuleFederationPlugin`) lets one build load modules from another build **at runtime**. Each build can be:

- A **remote**: it `exposes` modules (`"./Button": "./src/Button.jsx"`) and emits a small `remoteEntry.js` manifest.
- A **host**: it declares `remotes` (`checkout: "checkout@https://cdn.example.com/checkout/remoteEntry.js"`) and imports them like packages: `import("checkout/Cart")`.

**Shared dependencies** are negotiated at runtime: with `shared: { react: { singleton: true, requiredVersion: "^19.0.0" } }`, host and remotes use one copy of React instead of each bundling their own. Version mismatches produce warnings or fall back to separate copies, depending on settings.

Practical rules:

- The host must load shared modules asynchronously, so use a **bootstrap** pattern: `index.js` contains only `import("./bootstrap")`, giving the runtime time to negotiate shared versions. Otherwise you hit "Shared module is not available for eager consumption".
- Treat exposed modules as public APIs with versioning and contracts; independent deploys mean independent failures. Wrap remote loads in error boundaries.
- Type sharing, dynamic remotes and runtime plugins come from **Module Federation 2.0** (`@module-federation/enhanced`), which also works with Rspack, Vite and other bundlers.

Federation solves organisational problems (independent deploys of a large frontend) at the price of runtime complexity; a monorepo with shared packages is often simpler.
takeaways: Remotes expose modules via remoteEntry.js; hosts import them at runtime
Shared singletons keep one copy of React across builds
Use an async bootstrap entry for shared modules
Federation trades runtime complexity for independent deploys
pitfalls: Importing shared modules eagerly in the host entry, causing 'not available for eager consumption'.

quiz.q: What does `singleton: true` on a shared dependency ensure?
options: The dependency is bundled into every remote
Only one instance is loaded and used across host and remotes
It is loaded from npm at runtime
quiz.explain: Singletons are essential for libraries like React that break with multiple instances.

concepts.name: Writing loaders and plugins
concepts.summary: Write a loader as a source-transforming function and a plugin that taps compiler and compilation hooks via Tapable.
concepts.why: Custom build steps in large codebases are implemented as loaders and plugins.
concepts.body:
A **loader** is a function exported from a module that receives a file's source and returns new source. It runs in a loader context (`this`):

- `this.getOptions()` reads options (validate them with a schema).
- `this.resourcePath` is the file being processed; `this.addDependency(file)` makes webpack watch extra files.
- Return a string, or call `this.callback(err, content, sourceMap)` to also pass a source map; for async work use `const done = this.async()`.
- Loaders should be pure and cacheable (they are by default; `this.cacheable(false)` opts out). A `pitch` method can run before the chain in reverse order.

A **plugin** is a class with `apply(compiler)`. webpack's internals are built on **Tapable** hooks, and plugins tap them:

- **Compiler hooks** cover the whole lifecycle: `beforeRun`, `compile`, `thisCompilation`, `emit`, `done`, `watchRun`.
- A **compilation** represents one build of the graph. In `thisCompilation`, tap `compilation.hooks.processAssets` with a `stage` (e.g. `PROCESS_ASSETS_STAGE_ADDITIONAL`) to add or modify output files via `compilation.emitAsset` and `webpack.sources`.
- Hooks can be sync (`tap`), callback-async (`tapAsync`) or promise-based (`tapPromise`).

Use `compilation.errors.push(new webpack.WebpackError(...))` or `this.emitError` in loaders to report problems instead of throwing raw exceptions.
takeaways: Loaders: functions from source to source, with this.getOptions/callback/async
Plugins: `apply(compiler)` tapping Tapable hooks
Modify output in `processAssets` with the right stage
Report errors through webpack instead of throwing
pitfalls: Mutating assets in the `emit` hook (deprecated style) instead of `processAssets` stages.

quiz.q: Which hook should a plugin use to add a new output file in webpack 5?
quiz.explain: processAssets with an appropriate stage is the supported place to add or change assets.

concepts.name: Internals and build performance
concepts.summary: Understand the module graph, chunk graph and runtime, profile slow builds, and know when to switch to faster loaders or Rspack.
concepts.why: Large webpack builds can take minutes; understanding the internals points to the real fixes.
concepts.body:
Inside a compilation, webpack builds a **module graph** (modules and their dependency edges), then a **chunk graph** (which modules belong to which chunks, and how chunk groups load each other). The **runtime** in the output implements `__webpack_require__`: a module cache, a registry of module factory functions, and chunk loading via JSONP-style script tags or `import()` for ESM output. Reading a development bundle (`devtool: false`, `mode: "development"`) makes all of this visible.

Where time goes in slow builds, usually:

- **Loaders**, especially Babel and `ts-loader` with type checking. Replace with `swc-loader` or `esbuild-loader`, and type-check in a separate process (`fork-ts-checker-webpack-plugin` or `tsc --noEmit`).
- **Minification**: use the SWC or esbuild minifier via `TerserPlugin.swcMinify` / `esbuildMinify`.
- **Source maps**: expensive variants in development.
- **Too much work**: missing `include`/`exclude` on rules, large `resolve.extensions`, building unused locales (moment.js), and no persistent cache.

Measure before changing: `npx webpack --profile --json > stats.json` for the analyzer, `speed-measure-webpack-plugin` for per-loader timings, and `ProgressPlugin` for phase timing.

When a codebase outgrows these fixes, **Rspack** (Rust, webpack-compatible API and most loaders/plugins) often gives 5-10x faster builds with modest migration effort, while new projects typically choose Vite.
takeaways: Module graph -> chunk graph -> runtime with __webpack_require__
Loaders, minifiers and source maps dominate build time
Profile with --profile --json and per-loader timings
Rspack is the drop-in path to much faster builds
pitfalls: Optimizing config blindly without profiling which loader or plugin is slow.

quiz.q: What does `__webpack_require__` do with a module that was already executed?
quiz.explain: The runtime keeps a module cache, so each module's factory runs once.
